item.title: I don't need Bambu's 3D scanner, because my phone already scans parts well enough to print replacements
item.itunes:title: I don't need Bambu's 3D scanner, because my phone already scans parts well enough to print replacements
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
3D printing is an immensely enjoyable hobby, but it does have its annoyances. When I need to recreate a physical part without a design file, it can take forever to redesign it. It could be a plastic bracket or just a spacer. The usual process is to measure everything with calipers and build the geometry using CAD. And I'll be honest, I'm not very good at CAD.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

The standard recommendation is to buy a handheld 3D scanner. Indeed, I was intrigued by Bambu's upcoming 3D scanner. But there's one more way. This is where phone-based 3D scanning comes in. Instead of building a model from scratch, I can use my phone to capture an existing object and turn it into a 3D model. I've been checking out two apps: Kiri Engine and Polycam. Both these programs use photogrammetry to reconstruct objects from photographs, giving me a simple way to get physical objects into my 3D printing workflow.

My phone turns everyday objects into 3D models

Photogrammetry makes it easy to recreate objects without measuring them manually

The basic idea behind photogrammetry is pretty simple. Instead of measuring a model manually, you can take a series of photographs from different angles. The software then compares overlapping details across the images to determine the object's shape and reconstruct it as a 3D model.

That's useful for all kinds of objects, and especially objects with curves, which can be harder to measure manually. I don't know about you, but I find objects with curved profiles hard to measure effectively with rulers or calipers. Contours, curves, and smaller details are hard to get right. Photogrammetry gives me a much better starting point, since the measurements are largely correct and only need a bit of fine-tuning from me.

I've been using a combination of KIRI Engine and Polycam on my iPhone for this workflow. The apps take photographs of the object, preferably a full 360-degree capture, and turn them into actual 3D geometry that can be exported into other applications.

Polycam usually gets the most recommendations. The object-scanning workflow is simple and adaptable to many use cases, though I tend to stick to object-scanning mode. From there, all you really have to do is position the object in good lighting and move the camera around it while it captures photos. The app then processes these images into a textured 3D model that you can inspect or export. If you subscribe to the paid version, you can upload these images to the cloud for better processing, but I stick to the free version.

Generally, I prefer KIRI Engine to Polycam for ease of use. The basic workflow isn't all that different from Polycam. You're still taking photos of an object to create the model. But KIRI Engine differs with its Featureless Object Scan mode, which I found better at handling objects with reflective surfaces.

I stopped buying dedicated dash cams after realizing my old phone does it better

My old phone can replace a dash cam for free

When capturing photos of an object for a 3D scan, keep a few things in mind. Good light is paramount, and you'll want to capture all aspects of the object. That includes the underside and other areas that the camera can't necessarily see unless you turn the object around.

Of course, scanning is just the first step. Both KIRI Engine and Polycam will let you export your scans in an array of formats, including the obvious ones like STL and OBJ. You'll then want to import these into Blender or your choice of 3D modelling app. In my experience, the generated models are most of the way there, but not fully baked yet. Consider them a starting point.

Photogrammetry produces a mesh, not a parametric CAD design, which means you don't automatically get clean dimensions, properly aligned holes or editable features. A scan can look pretty good while still containing uneven surfaces, stray geometry or inaccuracies that become obvious when I try to fit the printed part.

Similarly, I wouldn't rely on a phone scan for components that need extremely precise tolerances. A replacement bracket might look identical to the original, but a mounting hole that's even slightly misplaced can make the entire print useless. You'll still want to use calipers to measure things like screw spacing and mating surfaces. The advantage is that those measurements let you correct the scan rather than blindly trusting the reconstructed geometry. More importantly, a dedicated 3D scanner tends to have the same limitations.

So, if you're going to correct the model anyway, you might as well start with an app on a phone you already have.

Your phone is a good enough 3D scanner for occassional use

A dedicated 3D scanner has its uses if you are regularly digitizing objects for professional work. But for occasional scans of replacement parts, spending money on dedicated hardware can be hard to justify. It certainly was for me.

Between KIRI Engine and Polycam, you have two great options to make the process more accessible. Even the free version is a good way to capture 3D models with a reasonable degree of accuracy. You'll still need to spend time checking the model and cleaning up meshes, but you don't have to start from scratch.

Beyond the time savings, the biggest advantage is that you're using a tool you already have instead of investing in another device. For occasional use, the results are perfectly reasonable and good enough as an alternative to buying a dedicated scanner.

KIRI Engine

KIRI Engine is a photogrammetry software that runs on the iPhone and uses the camera and LIDAR sensors to create 3D scans.

item.title: The best third-party Windows 11 Start menu app is getting even more customizable with widgets
item.itunes:title: The best third-party Windows 11 Start menu app is getting even more customizable with widgets
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Summary

  • Start11 v3 preview adds widgets inside the Start menu — 20+ interactive widgets for quick access.
  • New Taskbar Islands and grouping give a sleeker, more navigable taskbar than stock Windows 11.
  • Start11 is on sale during the preview window: price cut to $8 (was $10).

Okay, so I'll admit it; Microsoft has been doing better with the Windows 11 Start menu lately. The company has fixed most (if not all) of the pain points I had with it, and I have to give it credit for that. However, I do also love what Start11 is doing, which was my go-to app when I wanted something different. Now, Stardock has announced that a new version of Start11 has hit preview, and it contains widgets.

Start11 v3's release preview introduces widgets into the mix

Start11 somehow got even more customizable

Credit: Stardock

As announced on the Stardock blog (via Neowin), Start11 v3 has now hit release preview. One of the highlights for this version are widgets, which you can place directly inside the Start menu for a quick digest.

Here's how Stardock describes the new feature:

"Users can now add interactive widgets that display important information and provide quick access to everyday tools without opening another application. With more than 20 widgets available, including calendars, system monitoring, notes, clocks, and more, Start11 v3 makes the Start menu a more useful destination for getting things done."

Given how Microsoft is slowly adding customization options to Windows 11's native Start menu, Stardock needs to pull ahead to keep its position as one of the better ways to use it. Fortunately, it seems the company knows this, as Start11 v3 introduces new features that keep it ahead of the official offering. Taskbar Islands gives the UI a sleek, modern look, while the new taskbar grouping feature lets you put applications into little niches for an easier time navigating them.

To top it off, Stardock is reducing the price of Start11 from $10 to $8 during the release preview phase, so now's the perfect time to hop in if you're curious.

item.title: Sony turned the PS2 into a Linux PC 24 years ago, and it was way ahead of its time
item.itunes:title: Sony turned the PS2 into a Linux PC 24 years ago, and it was way ahead of its time
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
The PlayStation 2 holds an awful lot of memories for an entire generation — I was one of the millions of kids who played their first-ever 3D GTA game on the PS2. We may remember this console as one of the greatest ever, but Sony seemed to have considerably bigger ambitions for its little black box.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

In fact, 24 years ago, Sony sold an official kit that could turn your PS2 into an honest-to-goodness Linux PC, complete with the hardware and software needed to get started.

I'm not talking about some obscure homebrew project, either, or some exploit that made you jump through hoops. Sony actually wanted people to experiment with its hardware, and the result was far more interesting than you'd expect from a gaming console.

Sony actually sold everything you needed to turn a PS2 into a PC

The PS2 Linux Kit was a very real product

  • Credit: Wikimedia Commons / LegonXT
  • Credit: Wikimedia Commons / Deni Williams from São Paulo, Brasil / Brazil
  • Credit: Wikimedia Commons / Deni Williams
  • Credit: Wikimedia Commons / Xcion
  • Credit: Wikimedia Commons / Deni Williams from São Paulo, Brasil / Brazil
  • Credit: Wikimedia Commons / LegonXT
  • Credit: Wikimedia Commons / Deni Williams from São Paulo, Brasil / Brazil
  • Credit: Wikimedia Commons / Deni Williams
  • Credit: Wikimedia Commons / Xcion
  • Credit: Wikimedia Commons / Deni Williams from São Paulo, Brasil / Brazil

In 2002, buying a PlayStation 2 meant buying some games, memory cards, and a multitap, so four kids could crowd one couch and a CRT TV. Yet you could also buy a PlayStation 2 bundle that came with a 40GB hard drive, an Ethernet adapter, a VGA monitor cable, a USB keyboard and mouse, and two DVDs of Linux — for $200 on top of the $300 console.

You could even write your own software. Not to mention, you also needed a compatible computer monitor, even though Sony had done most of the heavy lifting. This kit also came in a Japan-only version in 2001, which technically makes a Japan-region PS2 today a quarter-century-old Linux machine.

It sounds incredible today, but Sony explicitly marketed it to Linux enthusiasts, programmers, and hobbyists who wanted to experiment with the PS2's hardware. This wasn't just aimed at gamers looking for another way to play their favorite titles. The official kit also included a hard drive and a network adapter. They were official PS2 peripherals that also enabled other console features, including online connectivity and hard-drive functionality in supported hardware.

Of course, there was a catch. You couldn't just hook the console up to any old television to have the PS2 Linux experience. Sony supplied a monitor adapter that required a compatible VGA display supporting sync-on-green (the green cable). That's what made this whole setup considerably more restrictive than just plugging a desktop PC into a monitor.

Two people used Claude to make a PS2 emulator that runs in your browser

You still need your own files, though.

1
By  Simon Batt

The machine was a proper computer under the hood

Sony wasn't handing developers a conventional desktop PC

Credit: Wikimedia Commons / Deni Williams

The PS2's internals were considerably more unusual than those of a conventional computer at that time. It had a 294MHz Emotion Engine, built around a MIPS III-compatible CPU core and supplemented by two vector processing units designed to accelerate the mathematical workloads games relied on. It also had just 32MB of RDRAM for system memory, alongside 4MB of embedded DRAM in its Graphics Synthesizer.

In fact, even though we're talking about a 24-year-old Linux computer, this distro still provided a proper Graphical User Interface working kernel, GNU development tools, GNU Compiler Collection (GCC), and X11 support through XFree86. However, one significant compromise remained: Linux developers didn't get unrestricted access to the Graphics Synthesizer's hardware acceleration.

Linux on the PS2 didn't mean that users could easily run unauthorized copies of PS2 games, though. Sony deliberately restricted direct graphics access. Naturally, this meant that developers couldn't just treat the console's GPU like an ordinary PC GPU, either. This peculiar arrangement made the kit interesting. After all, we're talking about Sony opening up a proprietary gaming machine to general-purpose computing, and they never surrendered complete control over the underlying hardware.

What was the PS2 Linux experience like?

An actual desktop operating system, with all the limitations you'd expect

Now, for a 24-year-old Linux machine, you'd expect the PS2 to offer only a command-prompt terminal to play around with. You'd be wrong, though, since Linux on the PS2 also offered a desktop GUI. Built around a Linux 2.2-era kernel and the XFree86 graphical environment, it let you connect to the internet, navigate the filesystem, and even run some applications like you would on a conventional Linux computer.

More importantly (and even more interestingly), Sony included a collection of development software, GCC, programming libraries, and other GNU tools. This meant that you could write, compile, and test your own code without ever needing another computer. Understandably, this was a compelling proposition for students and hobbyists interested in learning Linux, or even experimenting with the PS2's architecture.

It almost predicted today's handheld console environment

You can't not see the similarities

It's hard not to see this Linux PS2 machine as ahead of its time, given how closely its philosophy matches the direction the handheld PC market has taken. Devices like the Steam Deck aren't content with being locked-down gaming appliances today. They offer a relatively open computing environment, letting us install alternative operating systems, experiment with desktop apps, and treat that gaming hardware as a general-purpose computer.

Sony was exploring a remarkably similar idea two decades before Valve made it mainstream, albeit with considerably less powerful hardware and a much less polished experience.

The real innovation wasn't that the PS2 could run Linux, but that Sony was willing to support it officially. You didn't need to jailbreak anything, void your warranty, or hunt down obscure community patches. Sony had effectively given us permission to treat its gaming console like a computer. That's the part of the PS2 Linux experiment that feels genuinely ahead of its time.

It's a shame the console industry abandoned this vision

The idea, at the end of the day, was for too niche a crowd

Credit: Wikimedia Commons / Deni Williams

The PS2 Linux Kit wasn't an isolated experiment. Sony had already offered the Net Yaroze development environment for the original PlayStation, letting indie developers create their own games. Even the PlayStation 3 took it further with OtherOS, which let owners install Linux directly on their consoles.

Still, it had its limitations. For starters, the console's 32MB of system memory (and its 294MHz processor) weren't exactly powerful enough for heavy tasks or even desktop multitasking. Even lightweight applications such as early builds of the Mozilla web suite or the Dillo browser had to contend with the console's hardware limitations, and the restricted graphics acceleration made the experience far less capable than a regular PC.

The bottom line is that the PS2 Linux Kit will never replace your desktop. It was a developmental playground, and it wasn't meant to be a general-purpose computer.

I ran DLSS 5 on Rockstar’s GTA trilogy, and GTA 6 suddenly doesn’t feel that far ahead

Did we get GTA 6 before GTA 6?

3
By  Abhinav Raj

We'll probably never see anything like it again

Modern consoles are absurdly powerful compared to what we had in 2002, and yet manufacturers have become increasingly reluctant to let consumers do anything with that hardware beyond what their carefully curated ecosystems permit. It's backwards, really, to spend hundreds of dollars on a machine capable of sophisticated computing and still needing exploits and compatibility layers to run another OS.

I genuinely miss the idea that buying a gaming console could also mean getting an affordable playground for experimentation. Projects like the Steam Deck show that there's still an appetite for hardware that encourages tinkering, but Sony's PS2 Linux experiment remains a particularly fascinating reminder of what happens when manufacturers trust their customers to do more with the machines they own.

item.title: A $100 travel router is the easiest way I've found to reach my home server from anywhere
item.itunes:title: A $100 travel router is the easiest way I've found to reach my home server from anywhere
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
I don't travel often, but when I do, I'm always annoyed at the amount of setup I need to do once I get to the hotel. Along with my smartphones (yes, plural), a ROG Ally X running CachyOS, and my trusty MacBook, I also need to connect an Apple TV and the rest of the family devices to Wi-Fi. That's a struggle to begin with, especially if you get a per-room device limit, and then I always worry about security.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

I've also gotten heavily into self-hosting over the last few years, and want to be able to access those resources when I'm away from home. At first, I was juggling various remote access tools to get the connectivity I needed, but now I don't bother. All I pack is one more tiny device, a travel router that runs WireGuard to connect back to my home network. You can pick one up for about $30, although the model I have is a little more at $100.

Managing WireGuard across multiple devices used to be a nightmare — this changes everything

WGDashboard turns WireGuard's tedious setup into a 10-second QR code scan.

By  Dhruv Bhutani

WireGuard is great until you have many devices to manage

Every device needs its own peer, keys and client app and some can't run one at all

I've used so many different remote access tools over the last few years, and most have the same issues. Each device needs its own peer on the server, or access token. Some devices can't run a VPN at all, like my Nintendo Switch 2, or have fiddly setup for ensuring a persistent tunnel (like on SteamOS, where read-only root and Game Mode make it tricky).

Then, once you've got past that stage, the hotel puts another barrier in your way with a captive portal to sign in to before they can connect to a tunnel. That's easier said than done on some devices, and again, not every device will show the portal. It's just easier all-round to have a travel router log into the hotel Wi-Fi and act as a repeater to the rest of my devices, with a single WireGuard tunnel carrying all the traffic.

Remote access feels like the “final boss” of running a home lab, but NetBird made it a few clicks

Accessing your lab away from home shouldn't be complicated

1
By  Ty Sherback

I put my entire travel kit behind a travel router with WireGuard support

The only client config needed is on the router

I've got WireGuard set up on an LXC in Proxmox, so all I needed to do was to add one peer to the mix, and put those details into the GL.iNet's configuration pages. That's it. It uses the same port forward that all my other WireGuard traffic uses, connects as soon as the travel router is connected to a network, and rarely lets me down. Just remember to set the "block non-VPN traffic" option in the settings, so that all of your devices that connect to the router go through a tunnel.

Now when I get to a hotel, or I want to work from a coffee shop for a change of scenery, I connect the travel router to the Wi-Fi in repeater mode, sign in once to the captive portal, and let my devices auto-connect to the new hotspot. It takes minutes at most, and then I don't have to think about every device.

The only thing I have to consider is if the subnet used by the travel router is going to collide with either the hotel's network or my home network. By default, GL.iNet devices use 192.168.8.0/24, which isn't often used by anyone else. My home network uses 192.168.4.x through 192.168.7.x, because of how eero hands out DHCP, but that's still safe with this travel router. It's easily changed if I do find there's an issue with the local network, so I don't really worry about it.

Your router's default IP range is sabotaging your WireGuard VPN

The problem with defaults is everyone uses them

By  Joe Rice-Jones

I'd gladly pay for the convenience of not juggling configs

And don't worry about throughput. Hotel Wi-Fi is always the weak link

You might be wondering if throughput could be an issue, and I thought that too at first. But let's be real, when was the last time you had speedy Wi-Fi in a hotel or coffee shop? Or in a dorm room, or anywhere else that isn't your home network? Likely never, and that means Wi-Fi is always going to be the bottleneck, not your WireGuard tunnels.

The one-config-fits-all doesn't completely work, because things like your phone is always going to be moving in and out of range of the travel router. At least, unless you bring it along with you and plug it in wherever you have public Wi-Fi to use. Being powered by USB-C, all you need is a charger or a spare port on your laptop.

You can also use OpenVPN, ZeroTier, or Tailscale on newer firmware versions if that's your preference, or Tor, and GL.iNet has AdGuard Home built into the firmware so you can block ads. That might be a problem with some captive portals, so make sure you log in before toggling adblocking on.

I used a travel router at home for the first time recently, and now I understand why people love them

A travel router can both complement your main router as well as fully replace it.

9
By  Kazim Alvi

I don't chance it with hotel Wi-Fi and neither should you

While most of the reasons I pack a travel router are down to simplicity of setup, it's also a security feature. Open wireless networks aren't as dangerous as they used to be, but why take the chance if you don't have to? I'd rather err on the side of caution and bring a WireGuard-packing travel router to serve as the access point for my devices.

GL.iNet GL-MT3000

The GL.iNet Beryl AX is a great travel router that lets you have all your devices behind a VPN to your home network.

item.title: ChatGPT is getting GIF generation tools to make creating animated images a lot easier
item.itunes:title: ChatGPT is getting GIF generation tools to make creating animated images a lot easier
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Summary

  • Images 2.6 lets ChatGPT generate and edit GIFs in one step, like dancing cat reactions.
  • Adjust playback speed and inspect frames used to build the GIF.
  • Images 2.6 speeds up image creation; ChatGPT now makes 4B images/week.

Despite being around for decades now, the humble GIF is still the format of choice when creating silly memes to post on Facebook. However, asking an AI to help you make a GIF isn't as well supported as it could be. Fortunately, OpenAI is fixing that with a new tool that lets you generate and edit GIFs in ChatGPT. And, yes, the first thing they demoed with it is creating a cat meme, which is what single-handedly keeps the GIF format alive this side of the 21st century.

ChatGPT is getting GIF generation in Images 2.6

Making cat reaction GIFs has never been easier

As reported by The Verge, OpenAI is adding GIF generation to ChatGPT's Images 2.6 rollout. Beforehand, you couldn't just tell ChatGPT to make a GIF and have it complete the task in a single step. Now, with this new generator, you can ask for an animation in GIF format, and it'll make one right away.

The example OpenAI showed off involved someone asking, "Can you make a GIF of a cat dancing?", which at least shows that OpenAI knows exactly what people are going to be using this new feature for. Sure enough, ChatGPT makes the GIF, and the user can tweak how fast it plays and see the frames that went into making the animation.

Images 2.6 is more than just a GIF maker, though. OpenAI claims that it'll enable faster image generation, which is good news, because according to the company, ChatGPT churns out 4 billion images a week via the web app and the API, up from 3 billion in September. And now, with cat GIF memes as part of ChatGPT's repertoire, we'll likely see that number go up even further.

I used GPT Image to edit an image instead of Photoshop, and it got closer than I expected

Not every edit needs a slider

1
By  Nolen Jonker

item.title: This obscure Proxmox feature is built for data centers, but it's just as useful for hardcore home labs
item.itunes:title: This obscure Proxmox feature is built for data centers, but it's just as useful for hardcore home labs
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Between Proxmox’s new ARM image and OCI image-based containers, we’ve seen quite a few cool additions to the virtualization environment over the last couple of months, and that’s before I even include the new facilities added to the companion PBS and PDM services. However, one major feature that remained unnoticed by a large fraction of the community was the load balancer added to PVE 9.2.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

And truth be told, considering all the extra steps you have to take to set up a working cluster, let alone a high-availability one, it makes sense why there wasn’t a lot of fanfare in the community compared to, say, the OCI image support from Proxmox Virtual Environment 9.1. That said, this seemingly enterprise-tier feature is pretty useful for home lab setups, especially once you consider the sheer ease of deploying HA nodes with this lightweight platform.

I tried moving my home lab off Proxmox multiple times, but nothing came close to replacing it

Proxmox is in a league of its own when it comes to home lab projects

3
By  Ayush Pande

Before PVE 9.2, even the most over-engineered Proxmox clusters were prone to resource imbalance

Without manual rebalancing, your freshly recovered nodes would remain underutilized

Let’s say you’ve cobbled together a cluster from old parts and used ZFS replication (or better yet, Ceph distributed storage) to set up high-availability provisions for your setup. As long as you add your favorite virtual guests to the Resources tab and fine-tune their HA rules, you can rest easy knowing that Proxmox will move them to a different node if things go south on your primary workstation. Unfortunately, our problem begins after the first node comes back online.

You see, Proxmox uses a Cluster Resource Scheduler to balance the virtual machines and Linux Containers across high-availability nodes, but its old modes have a deal-breaking flaw: they aren’t concerned with moving virtual guests back to your original node. The basic mode, for example, assigns virtual guests strictly using the total HA resources assigned to it, while its static-load counterpart distributes the LXCs and VMs using the statically-allocated quotas. So, even though both nodes are well-equipped to migrate your Proxmox virtual guests to secondary nodes, they can’t rebalance the cluster when you restore the initial server.

As such, the freshly-revived workstation would remain idle, while the secondary nodes would end up with high resource utilization numbers trying to keep the virtual guests active. Up until PVE 9.2, the only way to solve this issue was to manually migrate the LXCs and VMs every time the primary workstation went down. Or, you could look into custom load balancer packages, but you’d have to deal with reinstalling them every time an update breaks your setup. Fortunately, Proxmox 9.2 got rid of this problem with the dynamic load balancer.

I ditched Proxmox VMs and moved heavy projects to LXCs, and superior performance wasn’t the only benefit

The benefits go way beyond speed

8
By  Ayush Pande

Proxmox’s new load balancer can automatically rebalance the cluster resources

It provides a neat solution to the lopsided cluster issue

Unlike the older CRS modes, the dynamic load balancer does precisely what you’d imagine from the name: it checks the existing resource utilization statistics of the virtual guests as well as the underlying nodes, and upon finding improperly-balanced nodes, it begins the LXC/VM migration tasks.

By default, it uses the brute force mode, which weighs CPU and memory usage equally across all nodes, and it’s what I’d rely on had it come out a few years ago when RAM was aplenty. But with the memory shortage forcing many home labbers (including yours truly) to work with RAM-starved systems, the TOPSIS mode makes cluster balancing easier for budget-friendly setups.

Unlike the brute force mode, TOPSIS prioritizes memory over CPU resources when calculating which migration tasks to perform. Specifically, it targets a 5:1 ratio for CPU-to-memory usage, and it bumps this ratio to 10:5 for CPU-to-RAM peaks. Personally, I’ve switched to the TOPSIS mode ever since I had to remove 16GB of DDR4 RAM from my primary workstation for the LLM-hosting experiments on my gaming machine.

Fortunately, building a Proxmox cluster is fairly cheap these days

You don't need to spend thousands on bucks just for a high-availability environment

Since we’re already on the subject of budget-friendly setups, PVE clusters don’t cost a fortune, especially when you compare them to HA nodes involving other virtualization platforms. Unlike ESXi, which requires you to have a paid license for a cluster, Proxmox lets you pair multiple nodes together in non-HA, ZFS replication, and Ceph configurations without forcing you to spend a dime.

Despite its solid VM and LXC-hosting provisions, Proxmox is extremely lightweight – to the point where you can repurpose any ol’ system as a PVE node. In fact, my ZFS replication cluster simply consists of an old Ryzen desktop paired with an N100 node, with a “mere” Raspberry Pi serving as the tie-breaker thanks to the QDevice package.

The new load balancer is so worth it for home labs

The dynamic load balancer may not be something most folks care about, but it's by far my favorite addition to Proxmox in 2026. Since I've configured my primary workstation to shut down when the power goes out, I'd typically have to move half my virtual guests back from the N100 every time there's a long outage in my backwater town. But with the dynamic load balancer set to TOPSIS mode, my PVE cluster handles the cluster re-balancing on its own.

Combine that with Proxmox's low system requirments, and building a PVE home lab becomes easier than ever.

3
By  Ayush Pande

Before PVE 9.2, even the most over-engineered Proxmox clusters were prone to resource imbalance

Without manual rebalancing, your freshly recovered nodes would remain underutilized

Let’s say you’ve cobbled together a cluster from old parts and used ZFS replication (or better yet, Ceph distributed storage) to set up high-availability provisions for your setup. As long as you add your favorite virtual guests to the Resources tab and fine-tune their HA rules, you can rest easy knowing that Proxmox will move them to a different node if things go south on your primary workstation. Unfortunately, our problem begins after the first node comes back online.

You see, Proxmox uses a Cluster Resource Scheduler to balance the virtual machines and Linux Containers across high-availability nodes, but its old modes have a deal-breaking flaw: they aren’t concerned with moving virtual guests back to your original node. The basic mode, for example, assigns virtual guests strictly using the total HA resources assigned to it, while its static-load counterpart distributes the LXCs and VMs using the statically-allocated quotas. So, even though both nodes are well-equipped to migrate your Proxmox virtual guests to secondary nodes, they can’t rebalance the cluster when you restore the initial server.

As such, the freshly-revived workstation would remain idle, while the secondary nodes would end up with high resource utilization numbers trying to keep the virtual guests active. Up until PVE 9.2, the only way to solve this issue was to manually migrate the LXCs and VMs every time the primary workstation went down. Or, you could look into custom load balancer packages, but you’d have to deal with reinstalling them every time an update breaks your setup. Fortunately, Proxmox 9.2 got rid of this problem with the dynamic load balancer.

I ditched Proxmox VMs and moved heavy projects to LXCs, and superior performance wasn’t the only benefit

The benefits go way beyond speed

Proxmox’s new load balancer can automatically rebalance the cluster resources

It provides a neat solution to the lopsided cluster issue

Unlike the older CRS modes, the dynamic load balancer does precisely what you’d imagine from the name: it checks the existing resource utilization statistics of the virtual guests as well as the underlying nodes, and upon finding improperly-balanced nodes, it begins the LXC/VM migration tasks.

By default, it uses the brute force mode, which weighs CPU and memory usage equally across all nodes, and it’s what I’d rely on had it come out a few years ago when RAM was aplenty. But with the memory shortage forcing many home labbers (including yours truly) to work with RAM-starved systems, the TOPSIS mode makes cluster balancing easier for budget-friendly setups.

Unlike the brute force mode, TOPSIS prioritizes memory over CPU resources when calculating which migration tasks to perform. Specifically, it targets a 5:1 ratio for CPU-to-memory usage, and it bumps this ratio to 10:5 for CPU-to-RAM peaks. Personally, I’ve switched to the TOPSIS mode ever since I had to remove 16GB of DDR4 RAM from my primary workstation for the LLM-hosting experiments on my gaming machine.

Fortunately, building a Proxmox cluster is fairly cheap these days

You don't need to spend thousands on bucks just for a high-availability environment

Since we’re already on the subject of budget-friendly setups, PVE clusters don’t cost a fortune, especially when you compare them to HA nodes involving other virtualization platforms. Unlike ESXi, which requires you to have a paid license for a cluster, Proxmox lets you pair multiple nodes together in non-HA, ZFS replication, and Ceph configurations without forcing you to spend a dime.

Despite its solid VM and LXC-hosting provisions, Proxmox is extremely lightweight – to the point where you can repurpose any ol’ system as a PVE node. In fact, my ZFS replication cluster simply consists of an old Ryzen desktop paired with an N100 node, with a “mere” Raspberry Pi serving as the tie-breaker thanks to the QDevice package.

The new load balancer is so worth it for home labs

The dynamic load balancer may not be something most folks care about, but it's by far my favorite addition to Proxmox in 2026. Since I've configured my primary workstation to shut down when the power goes out, I'd typically have to move half my virtual guests back from the N100 every time there's a long outage in my backwater town. But with the dynamic load balancer set to TOPSIS mode, my PVE cluster handles the cluster re-balancing on its own.

Combine that with Proxmox's low system requirments, and building a PVE home lab becomes easier than ever.

item.title: A guest Wi-Fi network isn't always the right place for your smart TV
item.itunes:title: A guest Wi-Fi network isn't always the right place for your smart TV
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Smart TVs have rightfully earned their bad reputation. Besides collecting data on the obvious stuff like what you're viewing, they run software that is often abandoned before the panel itself wears out, and they also sit on the same network as all of your other devices. One of the most common pieces of home network security advice is to put your TV on your router’s guest network as an isolation measure, but it's not always the best course of action. That isolation can break a lot of the features that make a smart TV worth using, and it doesn't actually tackle the privacy problem that you had to begin with.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover
The smart TV in your living room is training AI - here's how to stop it

The distributed web of compute is insidiously smart (and you should be angry about it)

3
By  Joe Rice-Jones

Guest networks are built to keep devices apart

They're designed to isolate users that may be untrustworthy

Fundamentally, a guest network's job is to give visitors internet access without giving them see anything on your home network. Most routers are capable of this, and do so by isolating guest clients from the rest of the network by default. Many routers also stop guest devices from talking to each other as an added protection.

It's exactly what you want for an acquaintance, but it can cause a problem for your smart TV, because a lot of the features it has relies on local network connectivity. Casting is the prime example of this: if you tap the cast button on any media from your phone, it'll begin to look for compatible devices using local discovery protocols like SSDP and mDNS, which only works with devices on the same network as the phone.

This includes things like Chromecast and AirPlay, but also affects companions apps. The Roku mobile app, for example, finds TVs through SSDP and then sends commands over HTTP. Any sort of local media share will also become unaccessible through the TV, but apps launched directly from the TV like YouTube or Netflix will be fine.

Why I stopped buying smart TVs, and what I bought instead

Remember when smart features worked for us, instead of against us?

15
By  Joe Rice-Jones

The usual fixes for this will undo the isolation

It's a bit of a catch-22

When casting breaks, the fixes most will reach for will tend to put things right back where they started. The most direct one is the router setting that lets guest devices access the local network. Turn it on and casting works again, but the TV can now reach your main network, which was the whole thing you were trying to prevent.

The other option is to switch the TV over to the router's IoT network, if it has one. That sounds like the right tool, but on many consumer routers it isn’t a security boundary at all. On my TP-Link router, its IoT network isn't separated from the main network at all. It’s handy for putting older 2.4GHz-only devices on their own SSID with their own security settings. As far as your other devices are concerned, though, the TV is still on your main network under a different name.

There is a Device Isolation feature on TP-Link routers, though, and it does what it says on the tin, but also breaks casting like the other fixes do.

I stopped my smart TV from tracking everything by changing this one setting

Disabling ACR on your TV is a simple process that protects your privacy.

7
By  Patrick O'Rourke

The best fix is to remove the TV from your network entirely

Use a dedicated media box

  • Credit: 
  • Credit: 

The risk most people are trying to mitigate isn't even an attacker trying to access their sensitive data via a smart TV vulnerability. It's usually about the TV itself tracking what they watch and gathering data on them. Many smart TVs use automatic content recognition, or ACR, to identify what’s on-screen. That includes content from a cable box or other device plugged in over HDMI, and the data goes back to the manufacturer for advertising. That traffic goes out to the internet, and a guest network allows internet traffic, so isolation does nothing about it.

Turning off ACR is one thing, but the cleaner fix is to just stop connecting the TV to your home network entirely. Most smart TVs can be set up without a Wi-Fi connection, which would eliminate any sort of data leaving the TV itself. Plugging a streaming box into it is how you restore connectivity for things like casting and streaming, and while it's not completely free of data collection, it usually won't have ACR. If you're truly concerned about privacy, the best move is to rely on an HTPC for home media consumption.

I ran a Pi-hole for a week and was genuinely disturbed by how much my TV phones home

Blocking the noise made everything faster.

By  Samir Makwana

Set up your TV based on how you actually use it

A guest network can be completely fine for a TV that doesn't ever get casted to, and putting it on one definitely won't hurt your privacy ambitions. Once you cast, use a phone remote, or play media from a local server, it starts working against you, and any of the normal fixes you'd deploy for those would nullify any privacy benefit. For most people, the better answer is to switch off ACR, or, better still, leave the TV offline and let a streaming box handle the "smart" part.

item.title: A free Photoshop alternative turned out to be a copy of an indie project, and now I check this before installing any open-source app
item.itunes:title: A free Photoshop alternative turned out to be a copy of an indie project, and now I check this before installing any open-source app
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Free Photoshop alternatives come up constantly in my work, and most of them get recommended on trust. Either there will be a reputable proprietary company behind the tool, or it's on GitHub with an open-source license attached, and for most of us that's pretty much where the vetting stops, admittedly myself included.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

PhotoSuite looked like a solid find when it showed up in September with Photoshop's classic layout and the open-source license to go with it. But about two weeks later, the developer of Photopea, the browser-based editor a lot of people use instead of paying Adobe and also one of my favorite editors, said it was built from his code. The story actually ended up getting a little messy, and it made me rethink what that open-source label is actually telling us.

An open-source Adobe suite built with AI is almost ready to replace the real thing

ArtCraft has seriously impressed me

6
By  Ty Sherback

What's the deal with PhotoSuite?

How a free Photoshop alternative got pulled from GitHub

I feel like Photopea needs a little background first. Ivan Kutskir has spent about 14 years writing it by hand, mostly on his own, and it runs free in a browser with ads paying for it. But it isn't open-source since Kutskir has never released it under an open-source license, and anyone who wants to host their own copy of Photopea has to pay him. Because it's a website, its code has to load into your browser for it to work at all, so anyone can technically see it, but that's very different from having permission to reuse it.

PhotoSuite went public on GitHub in late September. In early October, Kutskir opened an issue on its GitHub page accusing it of being his work repackaged, and pointed to code that matched a 2021 version of Photopea right down to oddly specific labels he came up with. The developer of PhotoSuite, going by eolix, admitted PhotoSuite began from an unofficial offline copy of Photopea that someone else had posted to GitHub. Their defense was that it's been rewritten since then, and that the README credited Photopea anyway.

From there, eolix renamed the issue to something softer and then banned Kutskir from it - a smidge dramatic, if you ask me, but I guess there's friction even in the open-source space. Shortly after, the Issues section was gone from the page entirely. PhotoSuite also started crediting a different app, PhotoCraft, as its foundation, which didn't hold up since people digging through the repo found PhotoSuite's own timestamps were older than PhotoCraft. I actually only recently tested out PhotoCraft myself, it's a pretty neat Photoshop alternative created mostly with AI, but it's still built entirely from scratch.

Kutskir filed a DMCA notice which is a formal copyright takedown request, and GitHub disabled PhotoSuite in mid-October along with the copies other users already made of it at that point. The notice also listed the offline Photopea copy PhotoSuite started from. eolix is still at it anyway, under a new name, PhotoSplice, which now says it's built on PhotoCraft instead.

I replaced the Adobe suite with a free open source alternative that Claude can control directly

Artcraft clones Adobe's apps for free, and Claude can run them for you.

9
By  Dhruv Bhutani

What I now check before trying new apps

You don't need to read code to vet an app

I did poke around in PhotoSplice a bit just to see how similar it actually is (though copied code doesn't necessarily mean the GUI will be the same). And admittedly, it does look pretty comprehensive and like the type of tool I cover here all the time. But luckily the dramageddon happened before I had the chance.

If you're like me and don't really know your way around a codebase, there are still ways you can vet a project before supporting it. One review site actually read PhotoSuite's code in early October and described it as readable and well-documented. Reading code clearly wasn't going to catch this, which is great news for me. Everything that gave PhotoSuite away was sitting on its GitHub page, and anyone can check for it.

First, start with how the project started. GitHub keeps a dated log of every saved change, called commits, and you can scroll back to the very first one. Most real projects start small and a bit messy before growing over months, whereas PhotoSuite's public history opened with roughly 1,000 files in a single go and four releases in five days. Some developers do work privately before going public, so this isn't immediate evidence of anything, but it might be something to take note of.

Then there's the license, which many tend to skip. When a README credits another app, I look up whether that app is open source itself. Photopea isn't, so PhotoSuite's open-source license didn't carry much weight, and a thank-you in the README doesn't count as permission.

There's also the Issues page to check, which is where people report problems, and I make a point of now opening the closed ones. Watching how a developer handles an awkward question can tell you a lot. If they'll ban someone for asking where the code came from, that's probably red-flaggy.

And lastly, the easiest check doesn't happen on GitHub at all. Literally just searching the app's name with words like "stolen" or "copy" on places like Reddit or Hacker News would have turned up the PhotoSuite story long before GitHub did anything about it.

I tried replacing Photoshop, Lightroom, and Acrobat with free vibe-coded alternatives, and they're surprisingly good

Got to give credit where credit's due

11
By  Mahnoor Faisal

There's also a point to be made about AI

Why this will probably keep happening

Kutskir believes AI did most of the work here. He's said a project like PhotoSuite could be made from Photopea's main code file in about two hours using Claude. eolix never confirmed using AI, so I'm treating it as a suspicion.

item.title: This overlooked metric can reveal CPU bottlenecks that GPU usage alone can't
item.itunes:title: This overlooked metric can reveal CPU bottlenecks that GPU usage alone can't
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
For as long as I can remember, GPU usage has been the one metric I've relied on to know whether my CPU is bottlenecking my GPU. I don't expect it to be pinned at 99%, but when the GPU is consistently sitting at 70–80% utilization, there's a good chance it's waiting on the CPU to catch up. Of course, other factors like FPS caps, V-Sync, and game engine limitations can also reduce GPU usage, but once you've ruled those out, the CPU becomes the likely culprit.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

That said, you're still making assumptions with GPU usage alone because it doesn't tell you how much time your graphics card actually spends working on each frame. And that's where GPU Busy comes in, a metric that Intel PresentMon brought into the spotlight. It tells you how many milliseconds your GPU actively spends working on a frame, so when you compare it with your frame time, you can get a much better idea of whether your CPU or GPU is the bottleneck.

GPU usage helps, but it isn't enough

Because it isn't a per-frame measurement like GPU Busy

There's nothing inherently wrong with monitoring GPU usage to identify CPU bottlenecks. If it stays close to 99% while you're gaming, that's usually a good indication that you're GPU-bound. The problem is that GPU usage isn't measured frame by frame. The percentage you see in MSI Afterburner or any other monitoring tool you use represents how busy your GPU was during a sampling interval. So, brief periods where your GPU is waiting on your CPU can get lost in the average.

Also, just because your GPU usage is hovering around 80% doesn't automatically mean your CPU is bottlenecking it. Enabling V-Sync, adding an FPS cap, or running into game engine limitations and RAM bottlenecks can also lower its utilization. That's why you're better off monitoring the GPU Busy metric using Intel PresentMon. You get a real-time measurement of how long your GPU is working on a frame, which you can compare to your frame time to see how much of that interval is spent on actual GPU processing.

You need to look at more than just GPU Busy, though

But PresentMon makes that easy by plotting it alongside frame time

GPU Busy is measured in milliseconds, but looking at that number alone isn't going to be helpful. You need to compare it with your frame time to better understand what's actually going on, and thankfully, Intel PresentMon lets you monitor both on the same graph. Let's say you're averaging 150FPS in a game, which works out to 6.67ms per frame. If your GPU Busy hovers around 6ms, it means your graphics card is spending almost the entire frame interval processing work, so you're probably GPU-bound.

Now, what if GPU Busy is lower at around 4ms? That's a 2.67ms gap between GPU Busy and frame time, suggesting your GPU finishes its work before the next frame is delivered. If you're seeing a similar gap across multiple frames, that could very well be a sign of a CPU bottleneck, but don't assume your CPU is spending that remaining 2.67ms preparing the next frame because CPU and GPU workloads can overlap. To narrow things down, you can lower your resolution or dial back some GPU-intensive settings. If GPU Busy drops further but your frame rates barely improve, you've probably hit your CPU's limits.

GPU Busy isn't the be-all and end-all either

But it still tells you more than GPU usage alone

Of course, just because GPU Busy is a lot lower than your frame time doesn't immediately mean your CPU is the bottleneck. As I mentioned earlier, FPS caps and V-Sync can prevent your GPU from working harder even if your CPU has no trouble keeping up. And let's not forget how slower RAM could also make your CPU wait for data, increasing frame times. Then, there's the fact that some games are simply CPU-bound because of engine limitations. For instance, Valorant doesn't fully utilize my RTX 4090 even though I have it paired with the 9800X3D.

But these are reasons to interpret the numbers properly, not dismiss the metric altogether. GPU Busy, just like GPU usage, cannot pinpoint a CPU bottleneck, but it does help you narrow things down. And in many cases, you're not going to be CPU-bound all the time. Some frames might take longer because of CPU-side stalls, while others could still be limited by your GPU instead. That's where GPU Busy has the edge over a utilization percentage. I still rely on both metrics, though, because I have MSI Afterburner running most of the time, and GPU usage quickly tells me something's off.

Start with GPU usage, but don't stop there

If you suspect a CPU bottleneck, the first metric I'd still recommend checking would be GPU usage because it's straightforward and something we're all accustomed to. Then, you can lower the graphics settings or enable DLSS to see if reducing your GPU's workload actually improves your FPS. If it barely moves, that's when I'd launch PresentMon and start monitoring GPU Busy. Just make sure you don't forget the other factors before you start blaming your CPU. At the end of the day, no single metric can pinpoint the actual problem. It's all about narrowing down the possibilities with the information you have.
